meta.description: A structured maturity assessment for cloud cost management. Answer 20 questions across six operational domains and receive a scored diagnostic with a prioritized improvement checklist.
meta.ogDescription: Cloud cost maturity assessment for PE diligence, board reviews, and 100-day planning. Score your cloud spend governance across six operational domains.

header.subtitle: A structured maturity assessment for cloud cost management. Answer 20 questions across six operational domains and receive a scored diagnostic with a prioritized improvement checklist. Scoring model informed by cloud cost governance patterns across PE portfolio companies.
landing.whoBody: This tool takes 5 to 7 minutes. Domains 3 through 6 require familiarity with cloud infrastructure. PE investors and executives should complete this alongside their engineering lead, or send them the link directly.

wizard.foundationalNote: This is a foundational domain. Scores here affect how results in later sections should be interpreted.
results.benchNote: Ranges reflect illustrative patterns from GST diligence and value creation engagements. Individual results vary based on team maturity and infrastructure complexity.
results.costContext: Cloud infrastructure as a percentage of revenue varies widely by company stage, business model, and architecture. Early-stage companies often run above 30 percent while scaling ahead of revenue. Mature SaaS businesses may converge below 10 percent. The trend matters more than the number - assess whether spend is moving in the right direction relative to revenue growth and whether the governance practices above are in place to sustain that trajectory.

method.scoring.heading: Scoring model
method.scoring.body: Each of the 20 questions is scored on a four-point scale: {a0} (0), {a1} (1), {a2} (2), {a3} (3). Domain scores are the percentage of points earned out of the maximum possible for that domain.
method.weighting.heading: Domain weighting
method.weighting.body: Foundational domains ({d1}, {d2}) carry 1.5× weight in the overall score. The remaining four domains carry 1.0× weight. This reflects the principle that visibility and attribution are prerequisites for effective optimization.
method.levels.heading: Maturity levels
method.levels.body: The overall score maps to four maturity levels: {reactive} (0–25), {aware} (26–50), {optimizing} (51–75), and {strategic} (76–100).
method.finops.heading: FinOps Foundation alignment
method.finops.body: The maturity levels map loosely to the FinOps Foundation’s Crawl-Walk-Run framework. {reactive} and {aware} correspond to the Crawl phase, where organizations are building foundational visibility. {optimizing} aligns with Walk, where active management is in place. {strategic} maps to Run, where cost governance is embedded in engineering culture. For more on the framework, see finops.org/framework.
method.flag.heading: Foundational flag
method.flag.body: If either foundational domain scores at or below 33%, a warning is surfaced. Low foundational scores indicate that higher-level optimization practices may be unreliable because the organization cannot see or attribute its spend.
method.recs.heading: Recommendations
method.recs.body: Recommendations are triggered when a question scores at or below a defined threshold. They are sorted by impact tier (high, medium, low) and can be dismissed as not applicable. Dismissed items are excluded from the printed report.
method.bench.heading: Benchmarks
method.bench.body: The benchmark ranges reflect illustrative patterns from GST diligence and value creation engagements. Individual results depend on company stage, team maturity, and infrastructure complexity.
method.snapshots.heading: Snapshots and comparison
method.snapshots.body: After completing an assessment, click Save snapshot to store your results in your browser. Up to three snapshots are kept; saving a fourth removes the oldest. Once you have two or more snapshots, a Compare button appears. It shows the two most recent snapshots side by side with per-domain score deltas. Use this to track governance improvements over time, for example between initial diligence and a 90-day post-acquisition review. Snapshots are stored in your browser only and can be cleared from the snapshot manager below the action buttons.
method.privacy.heading: Privacy
method.privacy.body: All calculations run entirely in your browser—no inputs are sent to our servers. Anonymous page-view and interaction analytics (Google Analytics 4) help us improve the tool. See our privacy policy for details.
maturityDesc.Reactive: Cloud spend is a black box with no visibility or controls.
maturityDesc.Aware: Some monitoring exists but systematic optimization is absent.
maturityDesc.Optimizing: Active cost management in place with meaningful room to improve.
maturityDesc.Strategic: Cloud spend is a managed, optimized discipline.

domain.d1.name: Visibility and Tagging
domain.d1.description: Can you see where the money goes?
question.q1_1.text: Are cloud resources tagged by team, service, and environment?
question.q1_1.rationale: Tagging is the single most important enabler of cost visibility. Without it, optimization efforts operate blind and cost attribution requires manual spreadsheet work.
question.q1_2.text: Do engineering leads have direct access to a cloud cost dashboard?
question.q1_2.rationale: When cost data is gated behind finance or a ticket queue, engineering decisions are made without cost context. Direct dashboard access closes the feedback loop between architecture choices and their cost impact.
question.q1_3.text: Is there a named owner who reviews cloud spend at least weekly and has authority to act?
question.q1_3.rationale: Cost optimization without ownership stalls. A named owner with review authority ensures spend anomalies are caught early and that optimization is a continuous practice, not a one-time project.
domain.d2.name: Account Structure and Attribution
domain.d2.description: Is spend structurally isolated so attribution is automatic?
question.q2_1.text: Are cloud billing accounts or projects segregated by environment (production, staging, development)?
question.q2_1.rationale: Environment segregation is the foundational first step in cost structure. Without it, non-production spend obscures production unit economics and makes cost anomaly detection unreliable.
question.q2_2.text: Are cloud billing accounts or projects segregated by service, application, or product?
question.q2_2.rationale: Service-level segregation enables clean unit economics per product, a key diligence requirement. It makes margin analysis possible without manual allocation.
question.q2_3.text: Are cloud billing accounts or projects segregated by team or business unit?
question.q2_3.rationale: Team-level segregation enables chargeback and showback models, creating natural accountability boundaries. Without it, cost ownership is ambiguous during scaling.
question.q2_4.text: Can finance or leadership pull per-product cloud cost reports without engineering involvement?
question.q2_4.rationale: Self-service cost reporting is a sign of structural maturity. If leadership needs to file a ticket to see spend by product, cost governance is bottlenecked on engineering bandwidth.
domain.d3.name: Right-Sizing and Utilization
domain.d3.description: Are you paying for what you use?
question.q3_1.text: Is compute utilization monitored with automated right-sizing recommendations surfaced to engineering?
question.q3_1.rationale: Without utilization monitoring, over-provisioning goes undetected. Automated recommendations turn data into action by flagging specific instances that are wasting spend.
question.q3_2.text: Have instances been right-sized using utilization data in the last 6 months?
question.q3_2.rationale: Right-sizing is not a one-time event. Workload patterns shift, and instances drift from optimal sizing. A recent right-sizing pass is a signal that cost optimization is an active discipline.
question.q3_3.text: What share of compute runs on reserved or committed pricing vs. on-demand?
question.q3_3.rationale: On-demand pricing carries a 30 to 60 percent premium over committed pricing for stable workloads. High on-demand ratios for predictable workloads indicate immediate savings opportunities.
domain.d4.name: Lifecycle and Waste
domain.d4.description: Do orphaned resources get cleaned up?
question.q4_1.text: Are automated policies in place to decommission unused or idle resources?
question.q4_1.rationale: Without automated cleanup, infrastructure accumulates over time. Stopped instances, unattached volumes, and idle load balancers silently drain budget.
question.q4_2.text: Do non-production environments scale down automatically outside business hours?
question.q4_2.rationale: Non-production environments that run 24/7 cost 60 to 70 percent more than necessary. Automated scheduling is one of the highest-ROI cost optimizations available.
question.q4_3.text: Are orphaned storage assets (volumes, snapshots, unattached IPs) identified and removed through automated policy?
question.q4_3.rationale: Orphaned storage is a common source of hidden waste. Volumes and snapshots from deleted instances persist indefinitely unless actively cleaned up.
domain.d5.name: Architectural Efficiency
question.q5_1.text: Is cost projection a required field in architecture decision records or infrastructure change requests?
question.q5_1.rationale: Embedding cost projection into ADRs normalizes cost as an architectural constraint. Without it, cost impact is discovered after deployment, when changing course is expensive.
question.q5_2.text: Has the team adopted serverless, spot, or preemptible compute for appropriate workloads?
question.q5_2.rationale: Spot instances can reduce compute cost by 60 to 90 percent for fault-tolerant workloads. Serverless eliminates idle capacity entirely. Not adopting these for suitable workloads leaves significant savings on the table.
question.q5_3.text: Is there a designated FinOps practice or cost champion within engineering?
question.q5_3.rationale: Organizations with a named FinOps champion consistently outperform peers on optimization outcomes. Without one, cost management defaults to ad hoc efforts that lose momentum.
domain.d6.name: Governance and Alerting
domain.d6.description: Are there guardrails, and do they fire?
question.q6_1.text: Do teams have defined cloud spend budgets with automated threshold alerts?
question.q6_1.rationale: Budgets without alerts are aspirational. Automated alerts at 80 and 100 percent of budget ensure cost overruns are caught before they compound.
question.q6_2.text: Is there an approval workflow for provisioning high-cost resources?
question.q6_2.rationale: Without approval gates, a single engineer can provision infrastructure that doubles monthly spend. A lightweight approval workflow for high-cost resources prevents accidental overruns.
question.q6_3.text: Are cloud costs reviewed as part of sprint or release planning cycles?
question.q6_3.rationale: Including cost in sprint reviews normalizes it as an engineering concern. It surfaces cost impact alongside velocity and quality, making cost-aware decisions part of the development rhythm.
question.q6_4.text: Does the team receive real-time alerts for anomalous cost spikes (e.g., greater than 20% week-over-week)?
question.q6_4.rationale: An undetected cost spike is an exposure event. Anomaly detection catches misconfigured services, runaway scaling, and unexpected data transfer before they become material budget events.
rec.r01.title: Implement a mandatory resource tagging standard
rec.r01.description: Define and enforce a taxonomy covering team, service, environment, and cost-center via IaC policy gates. Prevent untagged resources from reaching production.
rec.r02.title: Retroactively tag existing infrastructure
rec.r02.description: Audit current resources for missing or inconsistent tags. Prioritize production compute and storage, which typically represent 70 to 80 percent of total spend.
rec.r03.title: Deploy a cloud cost visibility dashboard
rec.r03.description: Implement AWS Cost Explorer, GCP Billing dashboards, or a FinOps platform. Engineering leads need direct access with no approval gate and no ticket required.
rec.r04.title: Establish a weekly cloud cost review cadence
rec.r04.description: Assign a named owner with authority to act. VP Engineering, FinOps lead, or CTO. Weekly review with a standing action item is the minimum effective frequency.
rec.r23.title: Segregate cloud accounts by environment
rec.r23.description: Separate production, staging, and development into distinct billing accounts or projects. This is the foundational first step: it enforces hard cost boundaries, prevents non-production spend from obscuring unit economics, and limits blast radius for cost anomalies.
rec.r24.title: Segregate cloud accounts by service or product
rec.r24.description: Create dedicated billing accounts per service or product line. This enables clean unit economics per product, a key diligence requirement, and makes it possible to identify which products are margin-positive without manual allocation.
rec.r25.title: Segregate cloud accounts by team or business unit
rec.r25.description: Assign distinct billing accounts or projects per team. This enables chargeback and showback models, creates natural accountability boundaries, and makes cost ownership unambiguous during organizational scaling.
rec.r26.title: Establish automated cost attribution by business unit
rec.r26.description: Implement account-level or tag-based cost allocation that maps spend to products and teams without manual reconciliation. PE buyers expect clean unit economics; manual spreadsheet attribution is a diligence red flag.
rec.r27.title: Audit commingled accounts for environment isolation
rec.r27.description: When all workloads share a single billing account, start by separating production from non-production. This is the highest-leverage first move: it immediately clarifies production cost baseline and enables non-prod scheduling savings.
rec.r05.title: Enable continuous utilization monitoring
rec.r05.description: Configure CPU and memory tracking across production instances. Flag right-sizing candidates automatically at under 30% average utilization over 14 days.
rec.r06.title: Execute a right-sizing pass on production compute
rec.r06.description: Downsize over-provisioned instances based on utilization data. A first pass typically surfaces 15 to 30 percent compute cost reduction with low performance risk.
rec.r07.title: Shift stable workloads to reserved or committed pricing
rec.r07.description: Identify predictable workloads and migrate to 1-year reserved instances or compute savings plans. Typical discount: 30 to 40 percent vs. on-demand.
rec.r08.title: Evaluate 3-year pricing for core stable infrastructure
rec.r08.description: For long-term stable workloads such as databases and core API tiers, 3-year reserved pricing can reach 60 to 70 percent discount vs. on-demand across major providers.
rec.r09.title: Implement automated resource lifecycle policies
rec.r09.description: Use cloud-native automation to identify and terminate stopped instances, unattached volumes, and idle resources on a scheduled basis.
rec.r10.title: Automate non-production environment scheduling
rec.r10.description: Configure dev, staging, and QA to power down outside business hours. Savings typically range from 60 to 70 percent of non-production compute cost.
rec.r11.title: Audit and eliminate orphaned storage assets
rec.r11.description: A structured audit of unattached volumes, obsolete snapshots, and unused IPs commonly surfaces $5K to $50K in annual waste at mid-scale.
rec.r12.title: Enforce resource TTLs for ephemeral environments
rec.r12.description: Tag environments provisioned for feature branches with time-to-live values. Automate teardown at TTL expiry to prevent infrastructure accumulation.
rec.r13.title: Embed cost review into architecture decision records
rec.r13.description: Require cost projection as a mandatory ADR field for infrastructure changes above a defined spend threshold. Normalizes cost consideration without adding process overhead.
rec.r14.title: Evaluate spot/preemptible for fault-tolerant workloads
rec.r14.description: Batch processing, CI/CD pipelines, and stateless services that tolerate interruption can reduce compute cost by 60 to 90 percent on spot instances.
rec.r15.title: Migrate event-driven workloads to serverless
rec.r15.description: Audit always-on instances running intermittent workloads. Scheduled jobs, webhook processors, and low-traffic APIs are prime serverless candidates.
rec.r16.title: Designate a FinOps champion in engineering
rec.r16.description: Assign cost ownership to a named individual, even part-time. Organizations with a named FinOps champion consistently outperform peers on optimization outcomes.
rec.r17.title: Create per-team budgets with automated alerts
rec.r17.description: Establish monthly spend budgets at team or service level. Configure alerts at 80% and 100% of budget to trigger owner notification before overruns.
rec.r18.title: Add forecasted spend alerts
rec.r18.description: Configure alerts on projected month-end spend in addition to actual spend. These fire while intervention is still possible, before the overrun materializes.
rec.r19.title: Introduce approval gates for high-cost provisioning
rec.r19.description: Define a threshold (e.g., $500/month estimated) above which resource provisioning requires engineering lead or FinOps owner approval.
rec.r20.title: Add cloud cost delta to sprint and release reviews
rec.r20.description: Include a cloud cost line in retrospectives and release reviews. Normalizes cost awareness without requiring a separate meeting.
rec.r21.title: Configure anomaly detection and cost spike alerts
rec.r21.description: Enable native anomaly detection or monitors for week-over-week spend increases above 20%. An undetected cost spike is an exposure event, not just a waste problem.
rec.r22.title: Establish a cost incident response playbook
rec.r22.description: Document the response procedure when an anomaly fires: who owns it, the investigation process, and available rollback or throttling options.
